title: Hub GCSE History Topic Checklist (Aligned to Edexcel 1HI0)
subtitle: Option 12: Warfare and British society, c1250–present and London and the Second World War, 1939–45

exam_structure.paper_name: Paper 1: Thematic Study and Historic Environment
exam_structure.overview: Section A tests the Historic Environment site (16 marks, 25 mins). Section B tests the Thematic Study across 4 eras (36 marks, 55 mins) plus 4 marks for SPaG.

sections.title: c1250–c1500: Medieval warfare and English society

topics.title: 1. The nature of warfare
points: Composition of the army (incl. the roles of the infantry, archer & the mounted knight); link between social structure & army command
Impact on warfare (strategy, tactics & combat) of new weapons & formations (incl. the longbow & schiltrons); gunpowder & the development of cannon; decline of the mounted knight

topics.title: 2. The experience of war
points: Recruitment & training of combatants in the medieval feudal army
Impact of war on civilians (incl. feudal duties & army plunder on civilian lives)

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: The Battle of Falkirk (1298): reasons for its outcome; the roles of William Wallace & Edward I
The Battle of Agincourt (1415): reasons for its outcome; Henry V

sections.title: c1500–c1700: Warfare and English society in the early modern period

topics.title: 1. The nature of warfare
points: Continuity & change: the composition of the army in the sixteenth & seventeenth centuries (incl. musketeer, pikemen, dragoons & the cavalry); development of a standing army
Impact on warfare of developments in weaponry (incl. new muskets & pistols)

topics.title: 2. The experience of war
points: Recruitment & training of combatants (incl. the New Model Army)
Impact of war on civilians (incl. recruitment & requisitioning)

topics.title: 3. Case study
points: The Battle of Naseby (1645): reasons for its outcome; Oliver Cromwell

sections.title: c1700–c1900: Warfare and British society in the eighteenth and

topics.title: 1. The nature of warfare
points: Continuity & change: the composition of the army (incl. the decline of the cavalry)

Impact on warfare of changes in weaponry (incl. rifles & bullets & the development of field guns & heavy artillery); impact on warfare of industrialisation(incl. steam- powered transport & the mass production of weapons)

topics.title: 2. The experience of war
points: Recruitment & training of combatants (incl. Cardwell’s army reforms & professionalisation)

Impact of war on civilians (incl. recruitment & requisitioning); impact on popular attitudes of the growth of newspaper reporting & photography in the nineteenth century, exemplified in the Crimean & Boer Wars

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: The Battle of Waterloo (1815): reasons for its outcome; Duke of Wellington
The Battle of Balaclava (1854): reasons for its outcome; Lord Raglan

sections.title: c1900–present: Warfare and British society in the modern era

topics.title: 1. The nature of warfare
points: Continuity & change: the composition of the army (incl. the growth of a logistics corps & specialised bomb disposal units)

Impact on warfare of developments in weaponry, transport & surveillance (incl. machine guns, tanks, chemical & nuclear weapons, the use of radar & aircraft); impact of computerised high-tech warfare; increasing use of motor & air transport & aerial support; Dealing with guerrilla warfare in the twenty-first century

topics.title: 2. The experience of war
points: Recruitment & training of combatants (incl. introducing conscription, national service, the recruitment of women & the development of a professional army)

Impact of war on civilians (incl. recruitment & the organisation of a Home Front during the First & Second World Wars & fear of nuclear war post-1945); Attitudes to Conscientious Objectors; influence of war reporting in the period on attitudes(incl. increased concern for casualties); Government use of censorship & propaganda in wartime

topics.title: 3. Case studies
points: The Western Front during the First World War & the Battle of the Somme (1916): the nature of trench warfare & war of attrition; Causes of outcome of the Somme; role of General Haig
The Iraq War (2003): reasons for its outcome; use of high-tech weaponry & surveillance techniques; London & the Second World War, 1939–45 The historic environment

topics.title: 1. London and the Second World War, 1939–45
points: Context of London in the Second World War (incl. its role in national government, significance as a target, importance as a port & industrial centre & its accessibility for German bombers); Preparations for war in London in 1939 & ongoing measures to safeguard the population: implementation of plans for evacuation, provision of Anderson shelters & gas masks

Nature of attacks on London; Attacks on the docks & industries of the East End (incl. Black Saturday (7 September 1940) & the V2 attack on Deptford (1944); Types of bomb used in 1940–41 & 1944–45, the scale of attack & extent of devastation(incl. problems dealing with incendiaries & V1 & V2 rockets)

Impact of the Blitz on civilian life in London: air-raid precautions (incl. underground stations & ‘Mickey’s shelter’); the impact of the South Hallsville School (1940) & Bethnal Green (1943) disasters; continuance of leisure activities in London(incl. dancehalls & theatre); Scale of disruption to daily life & work & government concerns about morale

London’s response to the war; continued presence of the Royal Family & government ministers; the Cabinet War Rooms; use of public spaces (incl. Victoria Park & the Tower of London moat, as part of the ‘Dig for Victory’ campaign)
Historical context of the Second World War: the nature & purpose of the Blitz; Government use of propaganda & censorship to influence attitudes about the Blitz

topics.title: 2. Knowledge, selection and use of sources for historical enquiries
points: Local source types: personal accounts & photographs, local newspapers, local council records
National source types: government records, newspapers, Mass Observation reports, newsreels, memoirs
Evaluating source strengths & limitations for historical enquiries
Formulating targeted follow-up questions for historical enquiries
Selecting relevant archival sources for follow-up investigations
